DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Thesis.** The KJV says the child Jesus was conceived in Mary, a virgin, by the Holy Ghost, and that Joseph did not beget him. Joseph was his father only as "supposed" and by legal standing. So no man was his biological father.

## 1. The genealogy breaks its own pattern at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". Every link in the line ends the same way, one man begetting the next.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb "begat" is *gennaō* (G1080, to beget, of a father). At the last link the text does not say "Joseph begat Jesus." It says "of whom [*ex hēs*, "out of whom," feminine singular] was born Jesus." The relative pronoun is feminine, so it points to Mary and cannot point to Joseph. Joseph is called "the husband of Mary" (*andra*, G435, husband), and the begetting formula stops there.

**[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law". The Greek *genomenon ek gynaikos* means "come to be out of a woman." Only the woman is named as his human source.

**[L4]** This stands on Matthew 1:16 [L1], with the feminine *ex hēs* [L2], and on Galatians 4:4 [L3]. The writer keeps "begat" for every father in the list and withholds it from Joseph, so Jesus' human origin runs through Mary alone.

## 2. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost," before Joseph and Mary came together

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The phrase is *ek pneumatos hagiou* (*ek*, G1537, "out of," marking source; *pneuma*, G4151, spirit; *hagios*, G40, holy). "That which is conceived" is *gennēthen*, from *gennaō*, the same verb used for each father in Matthew 1:2–16. The source of this begetting is the Holy Ghost, where the earlier links had a man.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." Joseph knew the child was not his, which is why he meant to put her away. The angel's word in Matthew 1:20 corrects him.

**[L4]** This rests on Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1], with *ek* marking the source and *gennēthen* matching the genealogy's own begetting verb [L2], and on Joseph's reaction in Matthew 1:19 [L3]. The begetting is attributed to the Holy Ghost and to no man.

## 3. Mary's own words and the angel's answer exclude a human father

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) is a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097, to know) is used here of relations between man and woman. The angel's reply gives the means as "the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee," and the word "therefore" (*dio*, G1352) makes the divine conception the ground of the title "Son of God."

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain." "Knew" is the ordinary idiom for conjugal union leading to conception. Mary's "I know not a man" therefore denies that union.

**[L4]** This rests on Luke 1:34–35 [L1], on *parthenos* and *ginōskō* [L2], and on the idiom in Genesis 4:1 [L3]. Mary has not known a man and conceives by the Holy Ghost's coming upon her, so no man's seed is involved.

## 4. Joseph did not know her until after the birth

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Ouk eginōsken* is "knew not," from *ginōskō* (to know), as in Luke 1:34. *Heōs* (G2193) means "until."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:18 says the pregnancy was found "before they came together." This confirms the order: the conception came first and the marriage union after the birth.

**[L4]** This rests on Matthew 1:25 [L1], with the idiom of *ginōskō* [L2], and on "before they came together" in Matthew 1:18 [L3]. At the time of conception Joseph had not had relations with Mary, so he could not have been the biological father.

## 5. Prophecy: a virgin, and the seed of the woman

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmah* (H5959). Matthew applies it with *parthenos* (G3933, virgin).

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43 uses the same *ʿalmah*: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water". The person meant is the one Genesis 24:16 calls "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed". The promised deliverer is called the woman's seed, not the man's.

**[L4]** This rests on Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23 [L1], with *ʿalmah* and *parthenos* [L2], and on Genesis 24:16 and 24:43 [L3]. The prophecy is of a virgin who conceives, and the fulfilment is stated in Matthew 1:18–25.

## 6. Answers in advance to what will be pressed

**"Thy father" and "son of Joseph."**

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought, was reckoned by custom."

**[L3]** Luke 2:49 is the child's own reply to "thy father" in Luke 2:48. He corrects it by naming "my Father's business."

**[L4]** This rests on Luke 3:23 [L1], on *nomizō* [L2], and on Luke 2:49 [L3]. Luke, who also records Luke 1:34–35, says Joseph was *supposed* to be the father. John 6:42 records what the crowd said, and Luke 2:48 records a household way of speaking. Neither states the fact.

**"Seed of David" and "fruit of his loins."**

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh".

**[L1]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ".

**[L3]** Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father". The writer speaks of descendants as being "in the loins" of an ancestor generations earlier.

**[L4]** This rests on Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30 [L1], with the "loins" usage of Hebrews 7:10 [L3], and on Luke 1:27, which names Mary a virgin and Joseph "of the house of David." Davidic descent "according to the flesh" can run through the mother, because the phrase speaks of ancestry and does not name Joseph as begetter. Matthew 1:16 says Jesus was born "of whom," that is, of Mary.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Matthew's genealogy uses "begat" (*gennaō*, to beget) for every father but ends with Joseph as "the husband of Mary, of whom [*ex hēs*, feminine, out of whom] was born Jesus." Footing: Matthew 1:2 and 1:16 [L1], *ex hēs* feminine [L2], Galatians 4:4 "made of a woman" [L3].
2. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost" (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, out of Holy Spirit), "before they came together," and Joseph knew the child was not his. Footing: Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1], *ek* as source and *gennēthen* [L2], Matthew 1:19 [L3].
3. Mary, a virgin who "know[s] not a man," conceives by the Holy Ghost's coming upon her. Footing: Luke 1:27 and 1:34–35 [L1], *parthenos* and *ginōskō* [L2], Genesis 4:1 "Adam knew Eve... and she conceived" [L3].
4. Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son," so he was not the begetter. Footing: Matthew 1:25 [L1], *ginōskō* with *heōs* "until" [L2], Matthew 1:18 "before they came together" [L3].
5. "Thy father," "son of Joseph," and "seed of David" are answered by Luke 3:23 "as was supposed" and by Mary's line of descent. Footing: Luke 3:23 [L1], *nomizō* "reckoned by custom" [L2], Luke 2:49 and Hebrews 7:10 [L3].
6. Christ had no human biological father: he was conceived in the virgin Mary by the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was his father only as supposed and by legal standing. Footing: Matthew 1:18–25 and Isaiah 7:14 [L1], *parthenos*, *ʿalmah* and *ek pneumatos hagiou* [L2], Genesis 3:15 "her seed" and Galatians 4:4 [L3].

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# Round 2: answers to the pressed rows, and the answer to Hebrews 7:14

I concede three narrowings at the start. They are discipline, and none of them touches the keystone.

1. No KJV row states Mary's tribe. I withdraw "Mary's line of descent" as a load-bearing part of D5 and rest the Davidic standing as shown in section 5.
2. Genesis 3:15 "her seed" is only supporting. Genesis 4:25 shows a woman's "seed" can have a human father, so the keystone does not stand on it.
3. Genesis 24:16 uses a different Hebrew word (*bethulah*) from Isaiah 7:14. The point stands on the KJV's own rendering of *ʿalmah* (H5959, a damsel or maid) as "virgin" in Genesis 24:43.

## 1. Against D1: Matthew 1:3, 5 and 6 against Matthew 1:16

**[L1]** Matthew 1:3: "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar". Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** In 1:3, 5 and 6 the subject is a man with the active *egennēsen* (G1080, "begat"). The woman then enters with *ek* (G1537, "out of"). In 1:16 the man is Jacob, who "begat Joseph". For the next generation the active verb is dropped and the passive *egennēthē* (G1080, "was born") is used, with the feminine *ex hēs* ("out of whom"). The formula is the same for 1:2 to 1:15 and it changes at the one place where the subject is Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20, margin: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]". The KJV margin gives the Greek *gennēthen* (G1080) as "begotten". So in Matthew's own book, the begetting of this child is assigned to the Holy Ghost, and the Greek verb for fathers' begetting appears with a source that is not a man.

**[L4]** This stands on Matthew 1:3 and 1:16 [L1], on the active-to-passive change in *gennaō* [L2], and on Matthew 1:20 with its margin "begotten" [L3]. The challenger is right that *ek* plus a woman fits a named father in 1:3 and 1:5. In those verses the father is stated as the subject of "begat". In 1:16 he is not, and 1:20 names a different source for the begetting. Galatians 4:4 and Job 14:1 fit every mortal birth. Only Matthew 1:16, with 1:18 and 1:20, withholds "begat" from the man.

## 2. Against D2: Matthew 1:19, and "born of God" in 1 John 5:1 and John 1:13

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L2]** *Paradeigmatisai* (G3856) is "to make a public example", that is, to expose to infamy. *Apolysai* (G630) is "to put away", used in its special sense of divorce.

**[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24 is the challenger's own row. It treats the betrothed as "his neighbour's wife" and speaks of her being put away. Matthew 1:19 shows a just man, with a wife found with child, who wants to put her away and not expose her.

**[L4]** This stands on Matthew 1:19 [L1], on *paradeigmatisai* and *apolysai* [L2], and on Deuteronomy 22:24 [L3]. If Joseph were the begetter, there would be no shame to avoid and no reason to put her away. The angel's reply gives the reason: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20). The "for" (*gar*, G1063) makes the Holy Ghost the answer to Joseph's fear. If the child were Joseph's, that answer would answer nothing.

**On 1 John 5:1 and John 1:13.**

**[L1]** John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."

**[L2]** John 1:13 uses *gennaō* of believers' regeneration (G1080 "figuratively, to regenerate"). Matthew 1:20 uses it of "that which is conceived in her", a conception in a womb, "found with child" (*en gastri echousa*, G1064 and G2192, "having in the womb") before "they came together" (Matthew 1:18).

**[L3]** Galatians 4:23: "he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise". The text treats a birth "by promise" as different from "after the flesh".

**[L4]** This stands on John 1:13 [L1], on *gennaō* as figurative regeneration versus a womb-conception [L2], and on Galatians 4:23 [L3]. Believers have human fathers and are also called "born of God", so that phrase is figurative. The phrase in Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 attaches to "found with child" and "conceived in her", which is a physical event. John 3:6 keeps the two kinds apart, and Matthew locates this child's physical conception on the Spirit's side.

## 3. Against D3: Luke 1:34, 1:32 and 1:35

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (G1352 with *kai*, "therefore also") adds a further ground to the title already given in 1:32. The word *kai* ("also") marks addition, so the title of 1:32 and the ground of 1:35 do not conflict. *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") is the verb of Genesis 4:1.

**[L3]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son". The angel speaks of a conception to come, and Mary's "How shall this be" asks about the means of that conception.

**[L4]** This stands on Luke 1:34 and 1:35 [L1], on *dio kai* and *ginōskō* [L2], and on Luke 1:31 [L3]. A betrothed girl who expected to conceive in the ordinary way after her wedding would not ask "How?" The angel answers with the means: the Holy Ghost comes upon her and the child is "born of thee". The answer names no man.

**The Solomon parallel (2 Samuel 7:14; 1 Chronicles 28:6).** Solomon's sonship is by choice: "I have chosen him [to be] my son" (1 Chronicles 28:6). Solomon also has a stated human father in David. Luke 1:35 gives the title a ground that Solomon's text never gives: "therefore also... shall be called the Son of God".

**The verbs.** *Eperchomai* (G1904, "come upon") in Acts 1:8 is said of the apostles, who were already born. In Luke 1:35 the object is Mary's womb conception, set by Luke 1:31 "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". *Episkiazō* (G1982, "overshadow") in Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15 names the presence and power of God or of a person's shadow. Luke 1:35 uses it with "the power of the Highest", which is the means of the conception.

## 4. Against D4: the order in Matthew 1:18, 24 and 25

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son".

**[L2]** *Synelthein* (G4905 *synerchomai*, "to come together", including to cohabit conjugally) comes before *heurethē* (G2147, "was found"). *Heōs* (G2193, "until") in 1:25 carries the abstinence to the birth.

**[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24: "his neighbour's wife". This is the challenger's own row, and it shows a betrothed woman bears the name "wife" before any union. So "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19) and "Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20) do not show a union.

**[L4]** This stands on Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 [L1], on *synerchomai* and *heōs* [L2], and on Deuteronomy 22:24 [L3]. Whatever the order of the taking, Matthew 1:18 dates the pregnancy "before they came together". Matthew 1:25 then carries the not-knowing from the taking to the birth. The challenger's "so Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal" is the unsupported step. Deuteronomy 22:24 shows that "wife" does not require union, and Matthew 1:18 puts the pregnancy first.

**"He called his name."** Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS". Luke 1:31 gives the same command to Mary: "shalt call his name JESUS". Naming is therefore not a father-only act.

## 5. Against D5, and the answer to Hebrews 7:14

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543, "was reckoned by custom", the form in Acts 16:13 "was wont"). The word means "by reckoning", and a reckoning is not a verdict on begetting.

**[L3]** Luke 3:38: "Adam, which was the son of God". Adam had no human father and was fully a man. Hebrews 4:15: "was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin". "In all things" in Hebrews 2:17 is qualified in the same book.

**[L4]** This stands on Luke 3:23 [L1], on *enomizeto* [L2], and on Luke 3:38 and Hebrews 4:15 [L3]. Luke puts "(as was supposed)" in his own voice. If Joseph were the begetter the parenthesis would be pointless. The word means "reckoned", which is what the public did in Luke 4:22 and John 1:45.

**The question: Hebrews 7:14, "evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda".**

**[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda". Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers".

**[L2]** *Prodēlon* (G4271, "plainly evident, manifest") is said of the tribe, and *anatetalken* (G393, "has risen, sprung up") names the rising, not a loins-begetting. The verse does not use *gennaō* (G1080), "begat", and it names no father.

**[L3]** Luke 2:4: Joseph went up to Bethlehem "(because he was of the house and lineage of David:)". Matthew 1:20, 1:24 and 1:25 show Joseph addressed as "son of David", taking Mary and calling the child's name. Esther 2:7: "Mordecai took her for his own daughter". Exodus 2:10: "and he became her son".

**[L4]** This stands on Hebrews 7:14 and Numbers 1:18 [L1], on *prodēlon* and *anatetalken* [L2], and on Luke 2:4, Matthew 1:20 to 1:25, Esther 2:7 and Exodus 2:10 [L3]. What is "evident" is the register, which counts by father's house. Joseph, "son of David", took the child into his house, and the register entered him there. Scripture elsewhere reckons a taken child as the son of the one who took him. This is the same custom Luke 3:23 marks by "as was supposed". Hebrews 7:14 therefore shows tribal standing by reckoning. It does not state who begot.

**On "seed" and "fruit of his loins" (C1).** Acts 13:23: "Of this man's seed hath God according to his promise raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus". God "raised" the seed, and Luke 1:32 says "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David". Hebrews 7:10's "his father" is Abraham, the great-grandfather of Levi, so the word "father" there covers an ancestor. The rows C1 and C2 name the tribe and house of David and Judah. They do not state that Joseph begot Jesus, and Matthew 1:20's "begotten... of the Holy Ghost" does.

## 6. Against D6: Isaiah 7:14 and the sign

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet". Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child".

**[L2]** *ʿAlmah* (H5959, "damsel, maid, virgin") is rendered "virgin" by the KJV in Isaiah 7:14 and Genesis 24:43. Matthew 1:23 uses *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin").

**[L3]** Isaiah 8:3: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz." That child is named differently from Immanuel and is a different sign.

**[L4]** This stands on Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:22–23 [L1], on *ʿalmah* and *parthenos* [L2], and on Isaiah 8:3 [L3]. Matthew states the fulfilment in 1:22 and 1:23, whatever near-term shadow Isaiah 7:16 casts. The keystone does not need Isaiah. It rests on Matthew 1:18 to 1:25 and Luke 1:34 to 35.

## Linking the challenger's chain

C1 and C2 are about the tribe and the house of David and Judah. The register reckons by the father's house, and Joseph's house is where the child was reckoned (section 5). C3 rests on Hebrews 2:14, "took part of the same", and Hebrews 2:17 "in all things... like unto [his] brethren". That likeness is in flesh and blood, and "in all points... yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15) shows it is not a likeness of origin. C4 states Joseph as the begetter, but no verse states it. Against that stand Matthew 1:16, 1:18, 1:20, 1:25 and Luke 1:34 to 35, which place the conception "of the Holy Ghost" and "of thee".

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" chain at Joseph. The active "begat" ends on Joseph, who is named by relation to Mary, and Jesus appears only as the subject of a passive "was born" "of whom". I drop "so Jesus' human origin runs through Mary alone" as a conclusion this verse reaches by itself.

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate, properly of the father, but by extension of the mother") stands twice in this verse: active for Jacob and Joseph, passive for Jesus. *anēr* (G435, "a man; husband") names Joseph as Mary's husband and not as the begetter of Jesus.
- [L3] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]". The margin puts the same verb, *gennaō*, on the Holy Ghost.
- [L4] The verb takes a father as its subject for every generation through Joseph (Matthew 1:16). At Jesus it changes, and the next verse that carries the begetting verb gives it to the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20).

Pressed rows:
- Matthew 1:3, "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar", Matthew 1:5, "Booz begat Obed of Ruth", and Matthew 1:6, "David the king begat Solomon of her [that had been the wife] of Urias". I grant that "of" names the mother beside a father. In each, the active "begat" takes the child as its object. In 1:16 "begat" takes Joseph as its object and Jesus is not its object, so the pattern differs where the narrowed limb says it does.
- Galatians 4:4, "made of a woman", Job 14:1, "Man [that is] born of a woman", Matthew 11:11, "born of women", and Luke 1:13, "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son". I grant that "born of a woman" is said of men with fathers. The narrowed link does not rest on that phrase.

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** The angel's ground in Matthew 1:20 attributes what is conceived in Mary to the Holy Ghost. I drop the claim that Matthew 1:19 states Joseph's knowledge of the begetting.

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] *gennaō* (margin "begotten"), *pneuma* (G4151, "spirit") and *hagios* (G40, "holy") stand in the verse.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". The narrator gives the same source before the angel speaks. Luke 1:35 names the same source: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee".
- [L4] The command "fear not" is grounded ("for") on a source that names the Holy Ghost and does not name Joseph.

Pressed rows:
- Matthew 1:19, "was minded to put her away privily". I grant that it gives intent and two grounds. The narrowed link does not ask why he was minded to do so.
- Matthew 1:24, "took unto him his wife". This fits, since he obeyed the command of 1:20.
- 1 John 5:1, "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him", and John 1:13, "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." John 1:13 sets "of God" against "the will of man". The row itself contrasts the two origins and does not set them side by side.
- John 3:6, "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." This names two kinds, and Matthew 1:20 names the Spirit's.
- Romans 1:3, "made of the seed of David according to the flesh", and Acts 2:30, "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh". *sperma* (G4690, "seed… by implication, offspring") states descent from David. The narrowed link does not deny that descent. It says what Matthew 1:20 assigns to the Holy Ghost.
- Galatians 4:23, "but he of the freewoman [was] by promise". The row sets promise against being "born after the flesh". Matthew 1:2, "Abraham begat Isaac", is a different row.
- 2 Samuel 7:14, "I will be his father, and he shall be my son", and 1 Chronicles 28:6, "I will be his father". The narrowed link is not built on "father" language here, but on "begotten" in Matthew 1:20.

**LINK 3: NARROWED TO:** Mary's question in Luke 1:34 is answered in Luke 1:35 by naming the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest. The answer names no man. I drop the claim that the verbs of 1:35 are lexically verbs of begetting.

Footing:
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"), *eperchomai* (G1904, "come upon") and *dynamis* (G1411, "power") stand in these verses.
- [L3] Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son". Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph".
- [L4] "How shall this be" asks for a means. The means given is the Holy Ghost and power, and a birth "of thee" follows the coming. No man appears in the answer.

Pressed rows:
- Luke 1:34 in the present tense. I grant it states her state when she spoke. The question concerns the conceiving still to come (1:31), and the answer supplies no man.
- Luke 1:27. It fits: she is called "a virgin" within the espousal.
- Luke 1:32, "the throne of his father David". The "therefore also" of 1:35 sits in the same verse as the Holy Ghost coming. I do not need it to be a verb of divine physical paternity.

# CLOSE ROUND: the defender's final defense

I hold D1 to D6 as declared. D4 is narrowed and D5 is kept with its footing restated. Where a challenger limb carries no footing for its inference, I say so. Where a limb is right, I concede it.

## D1: KEPT
Matthew's genealogy says "begat" for every father and changes the verb at Joseph.

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, to procreate, properly of the father) is the verb of the chain. Its last use is the passive "was born," and the relative is feminine, *ex hēs* (out of whom, a woman). Joseph is called *anēr* (G435, husband), not the one who begat.
- **[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."
- **[L4]** The chain runs on the begetting verb for every father. At the end it names Joseph as husband and names the woman as the one out of whom Jesus was born. Galatians 4:4 puts the same woman as the source.

## D2: KEPT

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:18 -- D2 --** "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- The challenger dates the finding before the taking and reads "came together" as the taking.
- The verse fixes the source of the child at the finding: "of the Holy Ghost." It does not say "of Joseph."
- So the source named is the Holy Ghost under either reading of "came together."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]." The word is *gennēthen* (G1080, begotten), the begetting verb of Matthew 1:2. The KJV margin renders it "begotten."
- **[L4]** In Matthew 1:2 *gennaō* is spoken of a father, and in Matthew 1:20 it is spoken of the Holy Ghost. So the begetting is credited to the Holy Ghost, and the child is "in her" (Matthew 1:20).

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:20 -- D2 --** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- The challenger says the "for" grounds the taking on 2 Samuel 7:14 ("I will be his father, and he shall be my son").
- That agrees with D2. In 2 Samuel 7:14 God says "I will be his father," and God is named as the father in the verse the challenger cites.
- **[L3]** Luke 1:35: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The "therefore" grounds the title in the Holy Ghost's coming.
- **[L4]** The "for" in Matthew 1:20 gives the reason Joseph need not fear. The reason is the origin of the child, which is the Holy Ghost. Had Joseph been the begetter, the "for" would have no force.

**ANSWER: 1 John 5:1 -- D2 --** "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him. [is born: Gr. has been born]"
- The challenger says "of God" sits beside human fathers, so "of the Holy Ghost" means covenant origin.
- **[L3]** John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." *thelēma* (G2307, will, volition) is named there, and "of God" is set against "the will of man."
- *gennaō* is also used figuratively, "to regenerate" (G1080). In 1 John 5:1 it is spoken of those who already exist and believe.
- Matthew 1:20 speaks of "that which is conceived in her," which is the coming-to-be itself.
- **[L4]** John 1:13 sets "of God" against "the will of man." Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 place the conception in her by the Holy Ghost's coming. So "of the Holy Ghost" in the nativity is the origin of the conception. It is not regeneration of a person already begotten by a man.

## D3: KEPT
- **[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The word is *ginōskō* (G1097, to know).

- D1 stands on the changed verb at Matthew 1:16.

## Against D1: Matthew's *ek* with a woman's name names the mother beside a begetter

**[L4]** This stands on Hebrews 7:14 and Numbers 1:18 [L1], on *anatellō ek*, *osphys* and *yalad* [L2], and on Hebrews 7:5, 7:10, Ezra 2:61 to 62 and Exodus 2:1 [L3].
- What is "evident" is a springing out of Juda.
- In the same chapter, that is a coming out of a father's loins.
- In the law it is a pedigree declared by the begetting verb, by the house of the fathers.
- A child taken into a house is reckoned by the house his seed came from.

So the defender's "Hebrews 7:14 therefore shows tribal standing by reckoning" covers the calling and leaves out the springing.

## LINK 1: SUPPORTED

**The premise.** "A child taken into a house is reckoned by the house his seed came from."

**Footing.**

- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood." The verse proves a man's standing for priesthood by his tribe.
- **[L3]** Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers." The law's register runs by the fathers' house.
- **[L2]** In Numbers 1:18, "declared their pedigrees" is *yalad* (H3205), "to bear young; causatively, to beget ... specifically, to show lineage ... declare pedigrees." The register's own verb is the begetting verb.
- **[L4]** The law's register is a register of begetting by the fathers' house (Numbers 1:18, *yalad*). Hebrews 7:14 argues priestly standing from that register ("of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood"). So the house that counts is the house the seed came from.

**Answer to Ezra 2:61, "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name".**

- The next verse gives the outcome. Ezra 2:62: "These sought their register [among] those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood. [were they...: Heb. they were polluted from the priesthood]"
- The man was called after the wife's house. When the register was searched by genealogy, the name taken from that house was put away.
- So the row shows the register by genealogy overruling a name taken from another house. It fits the link.

**Answer to Exodus 2:10, "and he became her son. And she called his name Moses".**

- The chapter has already fixed his house. Exodus 2:1: "And there went a man of the house of Levi, and took [to wife] a daughter of Levi."
- He "became her son" in Pharaoh's daughter's house. Yet he stands in the record of the house of Levi, the house of the man of Levi who begat him.
- The child taken into a house is still reckoned by the house his seed came from. It fits the link.

## LINK 2: SUPPORTED

**The premise.** "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal."

**Footing.**

- **[L1]** Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- **[L2]** "Seed" there is *sperma* (G4690), "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm'); by implication, offspring."
- **[L3]** The promise says where the seed comes from:
  - Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." Here *osphys* (G3751) means "procreative power."
  - 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- **[L3]** The canon's stated means of begetting is the husband knowing his wife. Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."
- **[L3]** Joseph and Mary are husband and wife from the espousal:
  - Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband." Here *anēr* (G435) means "husband."
  - Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Here *gynē* (G1135) means "a woman; specially, a wife."
  - Luke 1:27: "espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."
- **[L4]** The seed is out of a man's loins according to the flesh (Romans 1:3, *sperma*; Acts 2:30, *osphys*). Begetting is by knowing (Genesis 4:1). The one man the rows name, of the house of David, is her husband from the espousal (Matthew 1:19-20; Luke 1:27). So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal.

**Answer to Matthew 1:25, "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son".**

- The row opens with "And," joining it to Matthew 1:24: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife."
- *heōs* (G2193), "until," closes the not-knowing at the birth. The narration sets it after the taking.
- So the row covers the pregnancy inside his house. The union in the link stands before the taking, within the espousal. It fits the link.

**Answer to Deuteronomy 22:24, "the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife: so thou shalt put away evil from among you".**

- The law stones the man who humbles his neighbour's wife, that is, another man's betrothed.
- Matthew 1:19 names Joseph "her husband" (*anēr*), and Matthew 1:20 names her "Mary thy wife." She is Joseph's own wife, not his neighbour's.
- The just man (*dikaios*, G1342, "equitable") in Matthew 1:19 is the husband with his own wife. It fits the link.

**Answer to Matthew 1:18, "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".**

- The row dates the finding. Matthew names the coming together by what follows: "took unto him his wife" (Matthew 1:24).
- The verb there is *paralambanō* (G3880), "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself (in any familiar or intimate act or relation)."
- The law names the same step after the betrothal. Deuteronomy 20:7: "hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her."
- On "of the Holy Ghost": "of God" is said of believers who have fathers. 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God ... [is born: Gr. has been born]." So "of" with the Spirit marks origin in covenant and is said alongside a father.
- The finding comes before the taking, and the union stands within the espousal. It fits the link.

**Answer to Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]".**

- The conception stands before the taking. That is where the link sets the union: within the espousal, before the taking (Link 2).
- The command's "for" grounds the taking on the child being the seed God claims as his own: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14). That same verse 2 Samuel 7:14 was said of David's seed "which shall proceed out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12).
- It fits the link.

**Answer to Matthew 1:25 again.**

- The row's "And" ties its not-knowing to the taking just told in 1:24, and *heōs* sets the end.
- Start and end are both on the page. It fits the link.

**The narrowed premise.** A birth "by promise," set over against "after the flesh," has a named human begetter in the passage the defender cites: Abraham. I drop "in the very row."

**Footing.**

- **[L4]** Both sons are Abraham's (4:22). "By promise" (*epangelia*) marks the freewoman's son and stands against "after the flesh" (*sarx*). The promise-son still has his named begetter, so "by promise" sits beside a human father.

**Answer to Matthew 1:2, "Abraham begat Isaac".**

- The defender's own cross-reference gives the promise-son his begetter in the active verb, *gennaō* (G1080), "to procreate (properly, of the father...)."
- The son of promise in Galatians 4:23 is the son "Abraham begat." It fits the narrowed link.

## LINK 5: SUPPORTED

**The premise.** "In the same chapter, that is a coming out of a father's loins."

**Footing.**

- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:5: "though they come out of the loins of Abraham."
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."

- **[L4]** The loins of Abraham reach Levi and Juda only through each father's begetting in turn (Matthew 1:2). So the chapter's idiom, near or remote, is always a father's procreative power (*osphys*) passed down the fathers.

**Answer to Hebrews 7:10.**

- "His father" there is a forefather, Abraham. Levi was in his loins through Isaac and Jacob, each one a father who "begat" (Matthew 1:2).
- Being remote does not lift the idiom off the fathers. It runs down them. It fits the link.

- "Out of the loins of Abraham" is the same chain of fathers.

- Peter states the same throne by the same idiom. Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- Psalms 132:11: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne. [body: Heb. belly]"
- The forefather's loins reach the son through the fathers. The one father the rows name at the end of that line is "Joseph, of the house of David" (Luke 1:27). It fits the link.
